en.content:
The ongoing debate over Legislative Council’s “own role” reflects a healthy instinct: in an executive-led system, institutions must clarify boundaries without turning them into permanent rivals. When lawmakers discuss what LegCo should do—how far it should go in scrutinising policy, reviewing budgets, or proposing amendments—they are, at their best, looking for workable procedures that serve the public interest rather than partisan theatre. After all, legislation and oversight are not abstract ideals; they must function smoothly so that governance remains predictable and effective.

At the same time, the controversy is understandable. Some view LegCo as chiefly a legislative body that should avoid overreach, while others argue that meaningful checks and balancing require active engagement, including probing questions and rigorous scrutiny. The practical question, then, is not whether LegCo matters, but how it should matter—through timely deliberation, transparent committee work, and constructive coordination with the executive. A “middle way” should mean that LegCo’s role is neither decorative nor disruptive: enough autonomy to correct errors and improve policies, but within a framework that keeps decision-making moving.

This balancing act also connects to Hong Kong’s broader governance environment, including public sentiment around trust and institutional legitimacy. As journalists report a worsening press climate, the information ecosystem becomes more sensitive; policy scrutiny and public communication must therefore be handled with particular care. Even where there are political differences, procedures that encourage evidence-based discussion and disciplined questioning can reduce noise and focus attention on outcomes that affect ordinary residents—housing, livelihood support, and community safety.

Ultimately, the most productive direction is to treat LegCo’s role as something that can be refined through practice, not slogans. Clearer standards for agenda setting, stronger committee follow-up, and disciplined handling of motions can help translate debate into better governance. In an executive-led system, legitimacy comes from competence and responsiveness on all sides; a thoughtful middle path for LegCo is the kind of institutional maturity that Hong Kong should cultivate.
en.topic_title: A middle way for Legislative Council: Finding balance in legislature’s ‘own role’

zh.content:
立法會在「行政主導」的憲制架構下，應該扮演咩角色，一直都係香港政治討論嘅核心。今次有議員主動探討「立法會自身定位」，其實係健康訊號：證明制度唔係只靠對抗或口號去運作，而係面對現實去追問——立法會究竟要做監察者、政策參與者，定係程序守門人？喺現行體制下，立法會要有存在價值，就必須將權力用喺最能夠改善公共政策嘅地方，而唔係淪為純粹「跟車」或「擋車」嘅劇場。

問題係，所謂「平衡」唔等於模糊，更唔係各方各讓一步就當係解決。真正嘅平衡，係立法會要用制度設計去拉闊監督的深度：例如透過委員會研究、質詢同法案審議，把政府政策背後嘅假設、風險同執行細節拆開嚟講；同時，亦要承認行政機關喺政策整體性、資源配置與執行節奏上具優勢，所以立法會更適合發揮「補位」——集中打爛漏洞、改善成本效益、盯緊問責而唔係取代施政。簡單講：立法會唔應該追求萬能，而係要做到「有力而有界」。

但要做到呢點，立法會亦要提升政治理性。當議事變得過度敏感，甚至以程序作為替代政策討論，長遠會損害市民對制度嘅信任；相反，當議員能夠在爭議中仍然維持基本共同語言（如數據、時間表、成本、受眾影響），制度就會由「互不信任」轉化為「可被追問的承諾」。而制度能夠運作，亦會間接緩和外界對香港政治「失衡」嘅觀感：因為當立法會真係能夠讓政府交代得更清楚，社會自然更願意在分歧之上尋找政策落地嘅空間。

我嘅立場係：立法會應該走「監督先行、參與有限但實質」嘅路線——堅守程序正義，同時把審議焦點放喺公共利益嘅可驗證指標上，並建立更清晰嘅問責鏈。只有當立法會唔只係爭論「應唔應該」，而係追問「做得點、用得值唔值、出事誰負責」，平衡就會由口號變成日常。對香港而言，制度穩定並唔等於政治靜止；相反，穩定係讓分歧有出口、讓監督有成果。
